question: Can classifier training omit explicit cross-entropy computation and instead inject the output-space error directly at the logits, while retaining accuracy and reducing compute for softmax or alternative score activations?

key_findings.claim: With softmax, ISBE supplies exactly the standard softmax-cross-entropy gradient rather than defining a new learning rule.
key_findings.evidence: ISBE computes y = softmax(x) in the forward pass and calls backward on x with y minus the target. The appendix derives that same logit gradient for cross-entropy composed with softmax, so parameter updates match when batch reduction and scaling match.

anchors.section: A Cross-Entropy and Softmax Trick Properties

key_findings.claim: The sigmoid variant is also an existing objective in gradient form: independent one-vs-all binary cross-entropy with logits.
key_findings.evidence: For each class, ISBE injects sigmoid(x_i) minus target_i. This is precisely the derivative of softplus(x_i) minus target_i times x_i, the binary-cross-entropy-with-logits objective; omitting its scalar evaluation does not remove the implicit loss.

key_findings.claim: The tanh and hard-activation variants bypass the activation Jacobian, but the tested elementwise monotone rules still correspond to implicit separable surrogate objectives rather than to the displayed MSE.
key_findings.evidence: The backward call directly supplies F(x)-target. For an elementwise F, integrating each coordinate gives a scalar potential whose gradient is this error; for tanh it is log cosh(x_i) minus target_i times x_i. By contrast, the MSE plotted later would differentiate through F and include its Jacobian, which ISBE intentionally omits.

key_findings.claim: All reported accuracy differences are tiny and the paper's own interpretation is statistical parity, not a demonstrated improvement.
key_findings.evidence: Across N0 and N1, cross-entropy accuracies span 99.41%-99.61% and ISBE accuracies span 99.41%-99.66%; the largest tabled difference is 0.15 percentage points. The author explicitly states these differences are within statistical error, but provides no repeat-run uncertainty.

key_findings.claim: The timing tables do not establish an end-to-end training speedup of 3%.
key_findings.evidence: The measured quantity is tau = backward time divided by forward-plus-backward time, not total wall-clock time. Tau falls by 0.50-3.23 percentage points across configurations, but a lower phase share alone cannot prove that the total denominator decreased; hardware, repetitions, variance, and absolute times are not reported.

key_findings.claim: Theorem 1 is not valid as stated because its reverse implication silently assumes normalized outputs.
key_findings.evidence: The theorem declares only F:R^K to R^K, yet the proof of (2) to (1) invokes a 'unity condition' that is absent from the hypotheses. Functions y_j = a_j exp(x_j)/(C + sum_k a_k exp(x_k)) with C>0 satisfy the stated Jacobian and softmax-trick identity but sum to less than one, so they are not relocated softmax over the K classes.

key_findings.claim: The empirical support is restricted to MNIST and does not test the properties for which explicit probabilistic objectives matter.
key_findings.evidence: Two small convolutional architectures and five activations are evaluated only on MNIST-60K/10K. There are no tests of negative log-likelihood, calibration, class imbalance, soft targets, distillation, robustness, larger datasets, or modern architectures; sigmoid and tanh scores need not form class probabilities.

key_findings.claim: The proposed activation-selection heuristic is weakly supported and already has a reported counterexample.
key_findings.evidence: The paper recommends monotonicity, bounded range, and local Lipschitz behavior, then reports success for five hand-picked activations and more than a 10% degradation for p-norm normalization. No necessity theorem or systematic activation sweep links the heuristic to optimization or generalization.

method.core_idea: Remove the explicit scalar cross-entropy node and manually seed backpropagation at the classifier logits with normalized scores minus encoded targets.
method.mechanism: A selected score function F maps logits x to y. Instead of computing a scalar loss, training calls backward on x with the externally supplied vector y-target. For softmax this reproduces the fused softmax-cross-entropy logit gradient; for elementwise sigmoid, tanh, hard-sigmoid, or hard-tanh it supplies a deliberately Jacobian-free error rule. Targets are slightly blurred and remapped to the activation range when needed.
assumptions: A useful training rule need not expose or evaluate its underlying scalar objective.
Score monotonicity, bounded range, and local Lipschitz behavior are enough to generate useful output error signals.
MNIST accuracy is an adequate proxy for classifier quality despite the absence of probability and calibration measurements.
Changing cross-entropy reduction and manually supplied gradient scaling does not confound the optimizer comparison.
A smaller backward-time share implies a smaller total training time.

techniques.role: Seeds backpropagation with score-minus-target without evaluating a scalar loss node.
Uses the algebraic cancellation that makes the softmax-cross-entropy logit gradient y-target.
Treats normalized-score error as the logit gradient for non-softmax activations.
Blurs one-hot labels and maps them into [0,1] or [-1,1] to match the chosen score function.
Compares the fraction of forward-plus-backward time spent in backpropagation.

evaluations.setting: MNIST-60K training and MNIST-10K test with the N0 two-convolution/two-linear architecture.
evaluations.baseline: PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss with mean, none, and sum reductions.

evaluations.setting: MNIST with the deeper N1 convolutional architecture and its bias-enabled relocation variant Nr1.
evaluations.result: N1 cross-entropy spans 99.58%-99.61% versus ISBE 99.62%-99.66%; Nr1 cross-entropy spans 99.55%-99.64% versus ISBE 99.57%-99.69%, without repeated-run uncertainty.
evaluations.baseline: The corresponding architecture trained with CrossEntropyLoss.

evaluations.setting: N0, N1, and Nr1 forward/backward measurements across cross-entropy reductions and five ISBE activations.
evaluations.metric: Backward share tau of forward-plus-backward time.
evaluations.result: Tau is 59.56%-60.61% for N0 cross-entropy and 57.38%-59.07% for N0 ISBE; it is 53.92%-54.89% for N1 cross-entropy and 51.75%-52.68% for N1 ISBE, a tabled share decrease of 0.50-3.23 points.
evaluations.baseline: CrossEntropyLoss phase share for the same architecture, with no absolute wall-clock baseline.

evaluations.setting: MNIST under p-norm score normalization using the same architectures.
evaluations.metric: Classifier accuracy relative to the successful score activations.
evaluations.result: The paper reports performance more than 10% worse, despite the normalization satisfying several proposed qualitative criteria.
evaluations.baseline: Softmax, sigmoid, tanh, hard-sigmoid, and hard-tanh ISBE variants above 99.5%.

limitations: The evaluation uses only MNIST, two small model families, and apparently one result per configuration.
No seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, hardware, absolute runtime, timing repetitions, or variance are reported.
The timing metric is a phase ratio and cannot by itself support the claimed total-time saving.
The exact softmax case is only a re-expression of the established fused gradient, while the sigmoid case is the established one-vs-all BCE gradient.
No probabilistic metrics are reported even though non-softmax outputs generally do not sum to one.
Theorem 1 omits the output-unity hypothesis used by its proof and admits subnormalized counterexamples as written.
Theorem 2 is stated without proof and its elementwise vector-matrix product notation leaves the Jacobian scaling orientation ambiguous.
The illustrative PyTorch behavior for CrossEntropyLoss reduction='none' is underspecified because backward on a non-scalar loss normally requires an explicit upstream gradient.
The training hyperparameters, reproducible implementation, and code artifact are not fully specified in the paper.
failure_modes: Manual error injection can silently change gradient scale relative to mean or sum reduction and make optimizer comparisons non-equivalent.
Non-simplex scores can preserve argmax accuracy while producing unusable confidence estimates and poorly calibrated probabilities.
Hard activations keep receiving manually injected updates even when their true derivative is zero, so optimization behavior may be unstable outside MNIST.
A generic coupled score normalization may yield a non-conservative error field F(x)-target, leaving no scalar objective for monitoring or convergence analysis.
Framework-fused cross-entropy kernels may erase or reverse the presumed computational advantage of a custom manual-backward path.
The method may interact badly with soft labels, label smoothing, distillation, class weighting, or dense prediction unless target encoding and gradient scaling are rederived.
reusable_insights: Audit allegedly loss-free training rules by integrating the supplied update field; the scalar objective may be implicit rather than absent.
Compare manual-gradient methods to fused objective gradients at the exact tensor where backpropagation is seeded.
Separate removal of scalar loss evaluation from changes to the optimization objective.
Benchmark absolute step time and throughput with synchronized repeated measurements, not only the ratio of phase times.
Evaluate calibration and proper scoring rules whenever a classification method replaces simplex-valued probabilities.
State normalization constraints explicitly in Jacobian-characterization theorems; derivative identities alone may leave additive normalization constants free.
open_questions: Does a carefully fused ISBE implementation improve absolute throughput over production fused cross-entropy kernels on modern accelerators?
Which manually injected score fields are conservative, and what explicit surrogate loss does each one optimize?
How do ISBE variants behave on ImageNet-scale models, language models, dense prediction, and class-imbalanced datasets across multiple seeds?
Can non-softmax variants retain accuracy while matching cross-entropy on calibration, negative log-likelihood, robustness, and out-of-distribution detection?
What corrected characterization theorem results when simplex-valued output is added explicitly, and what is the proper matrix form of the dilated case?
Are any benefits left after matching gradient reduction, optimizer state, target encoding, and framework kernel fusion exactly?

competitive_landscape.title: Evaluation of Neural Architectures Trained with Square Loss vs Cross-Entropy in Classification Tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: Hui and Belkin compare explicit square loss against cross-entropy over major vision, NLP, speech, and Transformer settings with computational resources controlled. ISBE instead avoids scalar evaluation and tests manual score-error gradients only on MNIST; its plotted MSE is not its training gradient for nonlinear scores.

competitive_landscape.title: Estimating or Propagating Gradients Through Stochastic Neurons for Conditional Computation
competitive_landscape.difference: Bengio, Leonard, and Courville explicitly study derivative-bypassing estimators and name the straight-through estimator. ISBE's hard-activation variants similarly bypass local derivatives, but for deterministic classifier outputs and without estimator-bias or convergence analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: From Softmax to Sparsemax: A Sparse Model of Attention and Multi-Label Classification
competitive_landscape.difference: Sparsemax derives an alternative simplex-valued transformation, its exact Jacobian, and a matching smooth convex classification loss. ISBE permits arbitrary bounded monotone scores and bypasses their Jacobians, gaining simplicity but giving up sparsemax's explicit probabilistic and optimization semantics.

competitive_landscape.title: Are All Losses Created Equal: A Neural Collapse Perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhou et al. analyze when cross-entropy, MSE, focal loss, and label smoothing share neural-collapse solutions and test objective choice beyond one accuracy number. ISBE reports near-equal MNIST accuracy but does not analyze representations or identify the implicit objectives of its activation-specific gradients.

competitive_landscape.title: $f$-Divergence Based Classification: Beyond the Use of Cross-Entropy
competitive_landscape.difference: Novello and Tonello derive a principled family of alternative classification objectives from variational f-divergences and evaluate image and signal tasks. This broadens cross-entropy through explicit statistical objectives, whereas ISBE focuses on directly prescribing logit gradients and gives no risk or calibration interpretation for most variants.

competitive_landscape.title: BCE vs. CE in Deep Feature Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Li, Xiao, and Shen explicitly analyze one-vs-all binary cross-entropy against multiclass cross-entropy and show different absolute-versus-relative score geometry. ISBE's sigmoid rule has exactly the BCE-with-logits gradient, so this later work supplies an objective and feature-learning interpretation absent from ISBE's loss-unnecessary framing.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims cross-entropy computation is unnecessary for deep classifier learning, introduces ISBE as direct score-error backpropagation, characterizes softmax-trick activations, and reports unchanged MNIST accuracy with up to 3% time saved.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The softmax identity and manual PyTorch backward pattern are derived, five activations are tested on two MNIST architectures, and timing-share and accuracy tables are reported.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The useful engineering observation is that a known logit gradient can be supplied without evaluating its scalar loss. The central novelty is substantially narrower than the title: softmax ISBE is exactly fused cross-entropy in gradient form, sigmoid ISBE is exactly one-vs-all BCE in gradient form, other tested elementwise rules have implicit primitive losses, the uniqueness theorem is false without a missing unity assumption, and neither generalization nor end-to-end speedup is established.

reviewer_notes: All 18 cached pages, including both appendix theorems and proofs, were checked. Author-reported statements are separated from reviewer derivations. The implicit-objective observations follow by differentiating log-sum-exp, softplus, or coordinatewise primitives; the theorem counterexample follows by direct substitution into the stated Jacobian and softmax-trick equations. Competitor metadata was checked against current primary arXiv, OpenReview, PMLR, and NeurIPS records on 2026-08-23. This is a primary full-text pass, not an independent second-review verification.
